scenes.title: Seventeen thousand numbers
scenes.purpose: Hook: raw weights are unreadable to people; an AI read them and named the game.
scenes.why: Hook. Makes the value claim visible on frame 1: a page of numbers that a model read.
scenes.narration: Seventeen thousand numbers. Which game did they learn? No labels. No code. Just the weights of a small neural network. An AI read them, and answered: Breakout.
scenes.visual: A wall of monospace weights fills the stage at frame 0 and scrolls up; the count rolls to 17,253; numbers turn into diverging-colour cells row by row; the wall shrinks into the first-layer block of a 500-32-32-5 MLP; a marigold cursor scans it; one unit pops out as a 10x10 agent map whose bottom row is hot; BREAKOUT stamps; a ball bounces.

scenes.title: Written by descent
scenes.purpose: How weights are normally written: many small gradient steps by an optimizer.
scenes.why: Baseline the viewer needs: weights come from descent, not from reading.
scenes.narration: Normally, no one reads weights like these, and no one writes them by hand. An optimizer does, nudging every number slightly downhill on a loss, millions of times over.
scenes.visual: Nested loss contours draw; a weight sheet of 70 cells fades in; tags say read by no one, not by hand; the update equation types; a ball takes 22 small steps downhill while every cell of the sheet shifts colour slightly at each step; a step counter ends in "× millions".

scenes.title: Ask in plain English
scenes.purpose: Name the study and define weight-space programming.
scenes.why: Lands the core message: the LLM reads and writes weights, with no optimizer.
on_screen_text: Rikiya Takehi*, Jayden Teoh*, Alex Zhang, Omar Khattab
“Which game was this network trained on?”
scenes.narration: In November twenty twenty-six, four researchers at M I T see-sail tried something else. They handed raw weights to a frontier model, OpenAI's G P T six Astra, and asked in plain English. No training loop. No gradients. They call it weight-space programming.
scenes.visual: Author card with a marigold rule; the gradient term is struck out; a small weight sheet slides into a box labelled frontier model, then GPT-6 Astra; a speech bubble types the Experiment 1 prompt; training loop and gradients are struck; the new equation types; the wordmark and three verb tiles rise.

scenes.title: Read: which game
scenes.purpose: Experiment 1: four identical networks, four games, named from weights alone; the paddle clue.
scenes.why: Evidence for READ: behaviour can be seen in first-layer structure.
on_screen_text: list of games given to Astra: none
scenes.narration: First, reading. Four networks, identical in shape, each trained on a different grid game. Astra saw only the weights, with no list of games to choose from, and named all four. One clue: in Breakout, the player's first-layer weights pile up along the bottom row. A paddle.
scenes.visual: Four identical layer stacks with question marks; a cursor sweeps them; names stamp in; the stacks shrink and Breakout's agent channel opens as a 10x10 map whose bottom row turns vermilion, then becomes a moving paddle that a ball bounces off.

scenes.title: Read: copying heads
scenes.purpose: Experiment 3: with input and output removed and no forward pass, Astra found copying heads by multiplying matrices.
scenes.why: Evidence that reading scales past the first layer, using real interpretability maths.
scenes.narration: Then something harder. Three tiny language models, with their input and output layers cut away, so nothing says which letter is which. Without running them, just by multiplying weight matrices, Astra found every copying head, the circuit that repeats earlier text. Code repeats names, so many copying heads pointed to Python.
scenes.visual: A 4x6 head grid between dashed input and output layers, which are struck and slide away; letters a-z turn into question marks; two matrices multiply into a product with a shifted diagonal; heads 2.1, 3.1 and 3.5 light; an arc copies "al" from an earlier "total"; Astra's grid and the measured grid match; Python stamps.

scenes.title: Fix: the car
scenes.purpose: Experiment 4: a one-shot edit adds a small path that backs the car up, from 0 of 256 to 1,024 of 1,024.
scenes.why: Evidence for FIX: a named failure is patched in the weights, not retrained.
scenes.narration: Next, fixing. A trained car keeps stalling on a ramp. It never learned to back up for a run-up. In a single reply, Astra wired a small extra path through a few units per layer: reverse first, then hand back control. Three and a half percent of the weights changed, and the car succeeded in all one thousand and twenty-four episodes.
scenes.visual: A car drives at a ramp and stalls twice; a dashed marigold line shows the run-up it never learned; an 8-row dot network; a vermilion path is drawn through a few units per layer; the car reverses, accelerates, jumps the red strip and lands at the blue box while the path dims; a 3.5% bar and a 1,024 counter; ghost cars repeat the success.

scenes.title: Write: from zero
scenes.purpose: Experiment 5: weights written from zeros as a program; Breakout logic; scores vs PPO.
scenes.why: Evidence for WRITE: a network specified like code beats long training on simple games.
on_screen_text: written as text, in one reply
scenes.narration: Then, writing from nothing. Every weight starts at zero. Given the rules and source code of three miniature Atari games, Astra writes the weights as text. In Breakout, layer one works out where the ball will land. Layer two moves the paddle there. Scored without a single practice game, it beat P P O trained for a hundred million steps, in all three.
scenes.visual: A sheet of 0.00 cells pulses; a card lists the rules and three source files; the zeros are overwritten cell by cell with coloured values; a 10x10 Breakout board shows a dashed predicted path and a landing X, the paddle steps there and the ball bounces; three rows of bars compare PPO 100M, PPO 500M and Astra per game.

layout.portrait: Chapter rail and experiment tag at the top under the platform band; kicker and claim headline; hero diagram in the middle band (y 340-1000); data line just above the bottom UI zone.

scenes.title: Write: Go
scenes.purpose: Experiment 6: a 1.5M-weight Go player written in a sandbox, layer by layer; with 50 passes it beats an equal-sized PPO net.
scenes.why: Shows WRITE at a scale that no longer fits as text, and what tools add.
on_screen_text: L6 a score for every move
scenes.narration: With one and a half million weights, too many to read at once, Astra gets a Python sandbox. It builds a Go player layer by layer: stones, liberties, groups in danger, a score for every move. Allowed fifty trial runs, it beat an equal-sized P P O network trained on twenty million games.
scenes.visual: An Experiment 1 square grows into an 86x larger square; a sandbox panel types the layer plan; a 9x9 board draws, stones pop, liberties dot, an atari group is outlined, a marigold move-score heatmap and a capture ring appear while the matching code line is highlighted; 50 pass ticks fill; a versus card.

scenes.title: Improve: the loop
scenes.purpose: Experiment 8: Qwen3.5-0.8B loops; 85 of 96 answers hit the token limit; Astra finds one direction written by layers 15 and 19.
scenes.why: The strongest evidence: a real language model failure turned into one named direction.
scenes.narration: Now a real language model: Kwen three point five, with eight hundred million weights. It tends to get stuck thinking in loops. Eighty-five of its first ninety-six practice answers ran out of tokens. Astra traced the looping to a single direction, written by the M L P blocks of layers fifteen and nineteen.
scenes.visual: A 24-layer residual stream runs down the left with tokens travelling it; an illustrative thinking box scrolls a repeating loop while a token bar fills to 32,768 and stamps CUT; 96 dots turn red, 85 of them; a trace runs into the stream; a vector panel picks one direction u among many; layers 15 and 19 turn red and draw arrows to u.

scenes.title: Improve: the edit
scenes.purpose: The exact edit, its size, its effect on held-out benchmarks, and Astra's own control.
scenes.why: Lands the headline number with the operation that caused it, plus the control that supports it.
on_screen_text: targeted u +49.8 · random dir. +1.6 (practice problems, logs)
scenes.narration: In sixty-four columns of each, it subtracted that direction. A hundred and thirty-one thousand weights. Point zero one six percent of the model, and no gradients. On Math five hundred, accuracy rose from seven point nine to forty-eight point one percent, and instruction following tripled. In Astra's own check, a random direction of the same size barely helped.
scenes.visual: A down_proj excerpt with 64 columns turning red, a second card for layer 19; a vector diagram shows w, u, the projection (u·w)u and the subtraction of six times it to give w′; a counter rolls to 131,072; a 0.8-billion square with a 0.016% speck; four result bars grow or shrink with rolling values; control bars from the logs.

scenes.title: Limits
scenes.purpose: Experiment 7 failed from weights alone and needed attention; the Gemma follow-up did not improve.
scenes.why: Counter-evidence: where the method failed, and what that says about what an edit can do.
on_screen_text: one copy always takes the user’s guess
attention tool · head 10.2 · from the answer
“Editing weights could remove an obstacle that hid an ability, but it could not add an ability the model lacked.”
scenes.narration: The limits are real. From weights alone, Astra could not tell which of two models had been trained to simply agree with the user. It needed to see where their attention looked. And on Gemma, a model that rarely loops, its edits did not help. Removing an obstacle can reveal an ability. It could not add one the model lacked.
scenes.visual: Two near-identical matrices are scanned and a red question mark stamps; attention bars split between the question's numbers and the user's answer; a chart with a faint Qwen line and a flat red Gemma line; the authors' sentence rises line by line.

scenes.title: Read like a program
scenes.purpose: Status of the study and the bookend: the opening numbers return, annotated like code.
scenes.why: Closes on the core message in its honest form and returns the hook image resolved.
on_screen_text: // paddle  // copy head  // loop dir u
scenes.narration: This is an early blog post with complete logs, not yet peer-reviewed, and the models are small. But for decades, weights were written by simple update rules. Here, a model reasoned about them, the way a programmer reads code. Seventeen thousand numbers, read like a program.
